item.title: ATP Depletion, Cellular Order, and Energy Coupling
item.stimulus:
Researchers studied cultured mammalian cells to examine how cells depend on a continuous supply of energy. At time 0, the cells were moved from a normal growth medium into a medium with no glucose and no oxygen. Under these conditions the cells cannot make ATP by cellular respiration. At 2-hour intervals the researchers measured two things: the intracellular ATP concentration, and the percentage of cells with intact plasma membranes. Cells with intact membranes were counted as viable.

Time (h) | ATP (nmol per mg protein) | Viable cells (%)
0 | 8.0 | 98
2 | 5.2 | 95
4 | 2.4 | 80
6 | 0.8 | 42
8 | 0.2 | 11

In healthy cells, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to keep the K⁺ concentration higher inside the cell than outside. The researchers also noted that the enzymes these cells use for glycolysis have closely similar counterparts in many species of Bacteria and Archaea.
item.model_answer:
(a) Percent decrease = (8.0 − 2.4) / 8.0 × 100 = 5.6 / 8.0 × 100 = 70%. The ATP concentration decreased by 70% from 0 h to 4 h.

(b) As ATP falls from 8.0 to 0.2 nmol per mg protein, the percentage of viable cells falls from 98% to 11%. Living cells are highly ordered systems. To maintain that order and power cellular processes, their energy input must exceed their energy loss. With no glucose and no oxygen, the cells cannot make ATP by respiration, so their energy input stops while they keep using energy. Once ATP runs low, the cells can no longer maintain ordered structures such as intact membranes. This significant loss of order and energy flow results in cell death.

(c) (i) Hydrolysis of ATP is an energy-releasing reaction. The pump couples the energy released by ATP hydrolysis to the energy-requiring process of moving K⁺ from low concentration outside the cell to high concentration inside. This is active transport. (ii) The difference in K⁺ concentration across the membrane will decrease between 0 h and 8 h and approach zero. By 8 h, ATP has dropped to 0.2 nmol per mg protein, so there is almost no energy to power the pump. K⁺ continues to move passively down its concentration gradient out of the cell, and the pump can no longer move it back in, so the gradient dissipates.

(d) Glycolysis is a core metabolic pathway found with closely similar enzymes in Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. It is very unlikely that the same pathway evolved independently in every domain. The simpler explanation is that it evolved once in a common ancestor of all living organisms and was passed down to every descendant lineage. Its conservation across all domains is therefore evidence for common ancestry.

item.title: Blocked Step in a Sequential Energy-Releasing Pathway
item.stimulus:
A bacterium breaks down molecule A in a sequential metabolic pathway: A → B → C → D. Each step is catalyzed by a different enzyme. Enzyme 1 converts A to B, enzyme 2 converts B to C, and enzyme 3 converts C to D. Step 3 (C → D) releases energy, and the cell couples this reaction to the synthesis of ATP from ADP and phosphate. The bacterium uses ATP to power a membrane pump that moves H⁺ ions out of the cell against their concentration gradient.

Researchers grew the bacteria with a constant supply of molecule A. They then added inhibitor X, which binds to and blocks only enzyme 2. They measured the concentration of each molecule inside the cells just before and 30 minutes after adding inhibitor X.

Molecule | Concentration before inhibitor (μM) | Concentration 30 min after inhibitor (μM)
A | 50 | 52
B | 40 | 120
C | 35 | 5
D | 30 | 4
item.model_answer:
(a) Percent change = (120 − 40) / 40 × 100 = 80 / 40 × 100 = 200%. The concentration of B increased by 200%.

(b) The pathway is sequential, so the product of one step is the reactant for the next. B is produced from A by enzyme 1 and is normally used as the reactant for enzyme 2. Inhibitor X blocks enzyme 2, so B keeps being made but is not converted to C, and B builds up. C is made only from B by enzyme 2, so no new C is formed, while the existing C is still converted to D by enzyme 3. Therefore C decreases.

(c) The H⁺ concentration gradient across the membrane will decrease. With less C available, step 3 (C → D) occurs less often, as shown by the drop in D from 30 to 4 μM. Step 3 is the energy-releasing reaction coupled to ATP synthesis, so less ATP is made. The pump moves H⁺ against its concentration gradient, which is active transport and requires energy from ATP. With less ATP, the pump cannot keep moving H⁺ out, and H⁺ that leaks back in is not removed. Energy input no longer exceeds energy loss, so the ordered gradient runs down.

(d) It is very unlikely that the same pathway, with enzymes of very similar sequence, evolved separately in each of the three domains. More likely, the pathway was present in a common ancestor of all living organisms and was passed to its descendants in Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. It has been conserved because it is a fundamental way to obtain energy. Shared, conserved core processes like this support the idea that all organisms share a common ancestor.

item.title: Energy Coupling and Order in a Bacterial Cell Extract
item.stimulus:
Students study how cells power reactions that require energy. They prepare a cell-free extract from the bacterium Escherichia coli. The extract contains the enzyme that joins glutamate and ammonia to form the amino acid glutamine. Forming glutamine requires an input of energy. The students set up two tubes at 37°C. Each tube contains the extract, glutamate and ammonia. Tube 2 also receives ATP. They measure the rate of glutamine production.

Tube | ATP added | Rate of glutamine production (µmol/min)
1 | No | 0.2
2 | Yes | 4.6

In a separate experiment, living E. coli cells are placed in a medium with no usable energy source. A chemical is also added that blocks all ATP production by the cells.
item.model_answer:
(a) Forming glutamine requires an input of energy. In tube 2, ATP is hydrolyzed, which releases energy. The cell enzyme couples this energy-releasing reaction to the energy-requiring synthesis of glutamine, so glutamine forms much faster. In tube 1 there is no ATP, so there is no energy source to couple to the reaction and almost no glutamine forms.

(b) Percent increase = (4.6 − 0.2)/0.2 × 100 = 4.4/0.2 × 100 = 2200%.

(c) The cells will lose their internal order: they cannot keep synthesizing proteins, maintaining membrane gradients, or repairing structures, and they will eventually die. Living things are highly ordered systems, and by the second law of thermodynamics order tends to be lost. To maintain order and power cellular processes, energy input must exceed energy loss. With no energy source and no ATP production, energy flow stops, so order breaks down and the cells die.

(d) E. coli is in domain Bacteria and humans are in domain Eukarya. Because these distantly related organisms use the same sequence of glycolysis reactions, the pathway most likely evolved once in a common ancestor and was inherited and conserved in both lineages, supporting common ancestry of all organisms.

item.title: ATP Balance and Sequential Pathways in Yeast Cells
item.stimulus:
A researcher studies energy balance in yeast cells. Two identical yeast cultures are grown at 30°C in a medium containing glucose. Compound X is added to culture 2 only.

Compound X binds to the enzyme that catalyzes the third reaction of glycolysis and blocks its activity. Glycolysis is a sequence of enzyme-catalyzed reactions.

During the first hour after treatment, the researcher measures two rates in each culture. The rate of ATP synthesis is the rate at which the cells produce ATP. The rate of ATP use is the rate at which the cells hydrolyze ATP to power cellular processes such as protein synthesis and active transport.

Culture | Treatment | Rate of ATP synthesis (µmol per g cells per min) | Rate of ATP use (µmol per g cells per min)
1 | Glucose only | 12.0 | 10.5
2 | Glucose + compound X | 3.0 | 9.0
item.model_answer:
(a) Joining amino acids requires energy. The cell couples this energy-requiring reaction to ATP hydrolysis, in which ATP is broken into ADP and phosphate and energy is released. The energy released by ATP hydrolysis powers the formation of peptide bonds, so the overall coupled process can proceed.

(b) Percent decrease = (12.0 − 3.0) ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 9.0 ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 75%.

(c) The cells in culture 2 will be unable to maintain their highly ordered state and cellular processes such as protein synthesis and active transport, and they will eventually die. In culture 2 the cells use ATP at 9.0 µmol per g per min but synthesize it at only 3.0 µmol per g per min, so energy loss exceeds energy input. Living systems must have energy input greater than energy loss to maintain order and power cellular processes, and a significant loss of energy flow results in death.

(d) Glycolysis is a sequential pathway in which the product of one reaction is the reactant for the next reaction. When compound X blocks the third reaction, its product is not made, so the enzymes for the fourth and later reactions have no substrate. The later steps, including those that produce ATP, cannot occur, so the output of the whole pathway falls.

item.title: Energy Balance, Order, and Coupling in Growing Fish
item.stimulus:
A biologist studied how energy input affects the growth of juvenile zebrafish. Three groups of fish were fed different daily food rations for 14 days. Water temperature and all other conditions were kept the same. For each group, the biologist estimated three values. The first was the energy absorbed from food per fish per day. The second was the energy lost per fish per day, mainly as heat and in waste. The third was the percent change in body mass over the 14 days.

Group | Energy absorbed (J/day per fish) | Energy lost (J/day per fish) | Change in body mass over 14 days (%)
A | 120 | 80 | +18
B | 80 | 78 | +1
C | 40 | 75 | −12
item.model_answer:
(a) Net energy balance = energy absorbed − energy lost = 40 J/day − 75 J/day = −35 J/day. Over 14 days: −35 J/day × 14 days = −490 J. Each group C fish had a net energy loss of 490 J.

(b) Group A absorbed 120 J/day but lost only 80 J/day, a surplus of 40 J/day. Because energy input exceeded energy loss, the extra energy was available to build and maintain ordered structures such as new tissue, so the fish gained mass (+18%). Group C absorbed only 40 J/day but lost 75 J/day. Its loss exceeded its input, so the fish had to break down their own stored fats, glycogen and proteins to supply the missing energy. As a result they lost body mass (−12%).

(c) The group C fish would continue to lose mass and would eventually die. Energy loss would keep exceeding energy input, so the fish would use up their stored macromolecules. Once the reserves were gone, cells could no longer power the processes that maintain their highly ordered structure. A significant loss of order or energy flow results in death.

(d) Cellular respiration is an energy-releasing process. The energy released from glucose is captured by making ATP from ADP and phosphate. Joining amino acids by peptide bonds (dehydration synthesis) requires energy. The cell couples the hydrolysis of ATP, which releases energy, to this energy-requiring reaction. In this way the energy from glucose indirectly drives protein synthesis and growth.

item.title: Energy Coupling, Sequential Pathways, and Conserved Metabolism
item.stimulus:
A soil bacterium makes most of its ATP through a three-step metabolic pathway in which compound W is converted to compound Z. Each step is catalyzed by a different enzyme:

W → X (enzyme 1)
X → Y (enzyme 2)
Y → Z (enzyme 3)

ATP is produced during the step catalyzed by enzyme 3. The bacterium also builds the amino acid glutamine from glutamate and ammonia, a reaction that requires energy and does not occur on its own at a useful rate.

Researchers grew two cultures of the bacterium under identical conditions. They added a chemical that inhibits one of the three enzymes to the treated culture only. After 30 minutes, they measured the concentration of each pathway compound in both cultures.

Compound | Control culture (μmol/g cells) | Treated culture (μmol/g cells)
W | 2.0 | 2.1
X | 1.5 | 6.8
Y | 1.2 | 0.1
Z | 3.0 | 0.3

Genes encoding the enzymes of glycolysis have also been found in this bacterium, in archaea, and in eukaryotes such as yeast and humans.
item.model_answer:
(a) Making glutamine from glutamate and ammonia requires an input of energy. The bacterium couples this reaction to an energy-releasing process, the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate. The energy released by breaking down ATP is used to drive glutamine synthesis.

(b) Enzyme 2 (the enzyme that converts X to Y) was inhibited. In the treated culture X built up from 1.5 to 6.8 μmol/g, while Y dropped from 1.2 to 0.1 μmol/g and Z dropped from 3.0 to 0.3 μmol/g. W stayed about the same (2.0 vs 2.1). X is the substrate of enzyme 2, so blocking enzyme 2 lets X accumulate and stops formation of the compounds after it.

(c) Z decreased even though enzyme 3 was not the target. Enzyme 3 needs Y as its reactant, and Y is the product of step 2. When step 2 was blocked, little Y was made, so step 3 could not produce Z. This shows that each step uses the product of the step before it, so the pathway is sequential.

(d) I predict the cells will stop growing and eventually die. Because step 3 makes the ATP, blocking the pathway sharply reduces ATP production.
